title: Why can't you tickle yourself?
description: Go on, try: your own fingers on your own ribs will never produce the helpless laughter someone else's can. Your brain is cancelling the surprise — here is how.

body.heading: Two kinds of tickle
paragraphs: Scientists divide tickling in two. Knismesis is the light, feathery touch that makes skin crawl — a brush of grass, an insect's footstep — and most animals react to it. Gargalesis is the heavy, poke-and-wiggle tickling that produces helpless laughter, and it seems to belong to humans and other great apes.
Strangely, gargalesis almost only works when someone else does it. Your own hand, however sneaky, leaves you unmoved. The laughter is not in the fingers; it is in the surprise.

body.heading: The brain's cancellation service
paragraphs: When you move your own hand, a part of the brain called the cerebellum predicts exactly what the touch will feel like, moment by moment, and quietly cancels the sensation before it registers. Self-produced touch arrives pre-announced, so the skin's alarm never sounds.

Another person's hand cannot be predicted, so the touch lands at full strength — and the laughter that follows may be an ancient social signal, part panic, part play. Experiments with tickling machines show that even a tiny delay or wobble in the machine's movement can restore some of the effect: surprise is the active ingredient.

body.heading: Try it: the delay experiment
paragraphs: Tickle the sole of your own foot with a feather: mildly interesting. Have a friend do it with their eyes closed, changing speed without warning: quite another matter. You have just demonstrated the cerebellum's prediction service at work.

For the advanced version, hold a stick or ruler and use it to tickle your own foot — putting a tool between your hand and skin scrambles the prediction a little, and many people find it works slightly better. Slightly. Your brain is very good at its job.

takeaway: You cannot tickle yourself because your brain reads the spoiler first: it predicts your own touch and cancels the surprise that makes tickling work.
